source.author: Mario Mikulincer & Phillip R. Shaver
source.title: Attachment in Adulthood: Structure, Dynamics, and Change

method: Read in full (705 pages). Claims below are paraphrased from specific passages, cited by printed page. Deliberately excluded: the book's own assessment instruments (Appendices A-M, e.g. the ECR itself) beyond what Nimai's own ECR-R scoring already implements from the public instrument.

claims.paraphrase: When an attachment figure isn't reliably available, the primary strategy (seeking proximity) fails, and one of two secondary strategies tends to take over: hyperactivation, a 'fight' response that intensifies proximity-seeking (protest, demands for attention) in the hope of finally getting a response; or deactivation, a 'flight' response that suppresses signs of need and pushes the attachment system down to avoid the pain of an unresponsive figure. Hyperactivation develops from a partner who is sometimes responsive and sometimes not (partial reinforcement keeps protest going); deactivation develops from a partner who disapproves of closeness or need.

Attachment-focused therapy rests on the idea of 'earned security' (Berlin et al., 2008): adults who grew up insecure can become secure. The authors note the field should pay more attention to how this happens later in life, not only in childhood.

Citing Ainsworth (1991), the authors caution against treating anxious and avoidant attachment as simply 'bad': both are adaptive responses to the particular caregiving a person received, not flaws in the person.
